claims.claim: The Antikythera mechanism is an ancient Greek hand-powered orrery built in the 2nd century BC and discovered in 1901.
claims.excerpt: The Antikythera mechanism ( AN-tik-ih-THEER-ə, US also AN-ty-kih-) is an ancient Greek hand-powered orrery (model of the Solar System) built in the 2nd century BC and discovered in 1901.
claims.context: The device is identified as an ancient Greek model of the Solar System discovered in 1901.

claims.claim: The artefact was retrieved from a shipwreck off the coast of the Greek island Antikythera in 1901.
claims.excerpt: The artefact was among wreckage retrieved from a shipwreck off the coast of the Greek island Antikythera in 1901.
claims.context: The mechanism was found in a shipwreck near Antikythera.

claims.claim: In 1902, Spyridon Stais noticed that it contained a gear, prompting the first study of the fragment by Valerios Stais.
claims.excerpt: In 1902, during a visit to the National Archaeological Museum in Athens, it was noticed by Greek politician Spyridon Stais as containing a gear, prompting the first study of the fragment by his cousin, Valerios Stais, the museum director.
claims.context: Spyridon Stais and museum director Valerios Stais conducted the initial examination after spotting a gear.

claims.claim: The device was housed in the remains of a wooden-framed case of uncertain overall size 34 cm by 18 cm by 9 cm.
claims.excerpt: The device, housed in the remains of a wooden-framed case of (uncertain) overall size 34 cm × 18 cm × 9 cm (13.4 in × 7.1 in × 3.5 in), was found as one lump, later separated into three main fragments which are now divided into 82 separate fragments after conservation efforts.
claims.context: Physical dimensions and fragmentation of the device's case are recorded from conservation efforts.

claims.claim: Four of the fragments contain gears, while inscriptions are found on many others.
claims.excerpt: Four of these fragments contain gears, while inscriptions are found on many others.
claims.context: The physical components of the 82 fragments include gears and inscriptions.

claims.claim: The largest gear is about 13 cm in diameter and originally had 223 teeth.
claims.excerpt: The largest gear is about 13 cm (5 in) in diameter and originally had 223 teeth.
claims.context: Measurements describe the largest gear found within the fragments.

claims.claim: All the fragments of the mechanism are kept at the National Archaeological Museum.
claims.excerpt: All these fragments of the mechanism are kept at the National Archaeological Museum, along with reconstructions and replicas, to demonstrate how it may have looked and worked.
claims.context: The current location of the mechanism's pieces is the National Archaeological Museum.

claims.claim: It could be used to predict astronomical positions and eclipses decades in advance.
claims.excerpt: It could be used to predict astronomical positions and eclipses decades in advance.
claims.context: The physical capabilities of the device included predicting eclipses and astronomical positions.

claims.claim: It could also be used to track the four-year cycle of athletic games similar to an olympiad, the cycle of the ancient Olympic Games.
claims.excerpt: It could also be used to track the four-year cycle of athletic games similar to an olympiad, the cycle of the ancient Olympic Games.
claims.context: The device was capable of tracking ancient athletic game cycles.

claims.claim: Searches for items at the Antikythera wreck site in 2012 and 2015 yielded art objects and a second ship.
claims.excerpt: Two other searches for items at the Antikythera wreck site in 2012 and 2015 yielded art objects and a second ship which may be connected with the treasure ship on which the mechanism was found.
claims.context: Subsequent expeditions to the shipwreck site uncovered art and another vessel.
